tail_precision_rationale: M-DIFFREACH under adaptive escalation of the number of simultaneous progressions (single-attribute row up to a 3x3 with row and column progressions on two attributes) walks each child to the exact number of parallel progressions they can track. M-ERRTYPE distinguishes an off-by-one step (near-miss) or a previous-term periodicity slip from a random pick, refining where below the cut a child sits. M-CONSIST on an equal-difficulty twin shrinks the conditional standard error near the cut, and M-RTFIRST with M-RT credit reflective extraction of a multi-attribute progression over fast single-attribute pattern-matching.
age_rationale: Continuing a short repeating or +1 growing pattern is accessible to K-1 in single-row mode (big tap targets, no reading). 2-3 adds a single-attribute progression; 4-5 combines two attributes; 6-8 uses the 3x3 grid where row and column progressions must both hold with fixed-step rotation plus count. The K-8 tag reflects the shell spanning the full progressive-matrix difficulty range as one cognitive-model-driven bank (matching GF-006/GF-009 and, in single-row mode, GF-018). Continuation is developmentally accessible early, so the shell spans all bands.

adaptive.content_range: AB-AB and +1 single-row patterns (K-1) up to a 3x3 carpet with two-attribute row and column progressions and fixed-step rotation (6-8)
difficulty_levers: single row vs 3x3 grid (add the column axis)
step size and whether the step is constant or accelerating
distractor closeness: off-by-one step, previous term, wrong attribute
adaptive.notes: A progression grammar generates rows (and columns) and unlimited parallel forms; twin clones at equal difficulty enable consistency and drift checks; single-row items and full grids come from the same generator.

engagement_hook: Weaving a carpet that keeps growing - snapping the tile that continues the pattern triggers a satisfying continue-the-weave animation across the whole grid.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Avoid reading and numerals (use dots/shapes, not written numbers, for count); large tap options remove motor demands; key distractors to specific progression errors to block surface guessing; pair color with shape; keep pacing self-directed so processing speed does not contaminate the reasoning score; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Two Strangers
topics_techniques_covered: odd_one_out: several figures shown; select the figures that do NOT belong with the others (CFIT Scale-3 classification format requiring TWO odd figures)
odd_one_out: several figures share a generated rule except some; pick the ones that break the rule
odd_one_out: figures where most share a property and a minority do not; tap the strangers
odd_one_out: five figures shown; select the one figure that does not belong (single-stranger classic mode)
one_liner: Most of the figures follow a hidden rule; the child taps the TWO that do not belong.
interaction: Five to seven figures appear in a row or grid; all but two share a hidden rule. The child taps the two figures that break the rule (each tap lifts and highlights a figure; tapping a highlighted figure de-selects it). The child must select exactly two, then taps GO to confirm. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand scans across the figures pausing with a small nod on each that belongs, then taps firmly on the two that are different, which pop out of line together. One unscored warm-up (four triangles and two circles - tap the two circles) runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Requiring the child to find two violators rather than one is a documented way to push classification into the high-ability range without adding reading or knowledge load.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The scored items require selecting exactly two strangers, and their shared-attribute overlap with the majority is a difficulty lever, following the CFIT Scale-3 design.
learning_science.source: Cattell (1963), Journal of Educational Psychology 54(1)

learning_science.why: The slowest, not fastest, responses across several quick trials index ability, so consistency matters more than peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The type runs several short trials and logs RT variability rather than crediting raw speed; two-target selection also blocks single-guess luck.
learning_science.source: Coyle (2003), Intelligence 31(6)

learning_science.why: A two-target response yields graded evidence from one item (0, 1, or 2 correct strangers).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring is per-stranger-found so finding one of two earns graded credit and behaves like more than one dichotomous item.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: Finding TWO strangers turns one item into graded evidence: M-POLY scores 0/1/2 correct so a child who catches one violator but misses the subtler one is placed between full and zero - precisely the near-cut resolution a single right/wrong bit cannot give. M-ERRTYPE tags which shared attribute a wrong tap honored (a defensible alternative grouping vs a salience-driven error), and M-EXPLORE logs how many figures the child inspected before committing, separating systematic feature-checking from first-glance guessing. M-RTFIRST indexes rule-induction time before acting.
age_rationale: Holding the majority rule in mind while searching for two violators exceeds K-1 working memory; K-1 odd-one-out is served by the single-stranger FLU-ODDBALL-01. 2-3 uses an obvious single-feature rule with two clear strangers; 4-5 raises the attribute overlap; 6-8 uses a subtle generated rule where the two strangers each break it in a different, non-salient way (matching the 6-8 GF-023/GF-024 items). Single-tap selection and no reading keep it accessible from grade 2.

adaptive.content_range: two obvious single-feature strangers among five (grades 2-3) up to two subtle multi-attribute strangers among seven (6-8)
difficulty_levers: how the two strangers differ (same violation vs two different violations)
adaptive.notes: Generated by sampling a rule for the majority then perturbing exactly two figures with keyed violations; unlimited clones and easy difficulty titration; short trials give many RT samples; a single-stranger classic mode uses the same generator for the youngest content.

engagement_hook: A find-the-two-imposters hunt - spotting both strangers and watching them pop out together is a satisfying detective payoff, and quick rounds create a light game rhythm.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ensure exactly two figures are defensibly the strangers (audit for alternative valid groupings) so partial-credit and near-miss coding are meaningful; require exactly two selections so guessing one is not rewarded as success; pair color with shape; do not reward mere speed; single large tap targets remove motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Double Match
topics_techniques_covered: figure_classification: pick the figure that shares BOTH generated attributes (e.g. the same shape count AND the same fill) with the target set
figure_classification: four figures share one generated attribute value; pick the one that also fits
figure_classification: three figures share a hidden property; pick the figure that belongs with the set
nonverbal_deduction: choose the figure where a conjunctive spatial/attribute condition holds (belongs to set A AND set B, like a dot inside the circle AND inside the square)
one_liner: Two example groups each share a secret feature; the child picks the figure that belongs to BOTH groups at once.
interaction: Two overlapping rings are shown, each already holding a few example figures (the left ring's members share one feature, the right ring's members share another); the overlap region is empty. Four candidate figures sit below. The child taps the candidate that belongs in the overlap (it shares the left feature AND the right feature); it snaps into the overlap zone (tap another to swap). An optional quick two-icon confidence tap (a star for sure, a wavy hand for not sure) appears, then GO submits. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand circles the left ring's members (highlighting their shared feature), then the right ring's members (their shared feature), then taps the candidate that has both and drops it into the overlap, which glows to accept. One unscored warm-up (left ring = red things, right ring = circles; pick the red circle) runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: A concept defined by the joint presence of two attributes is harder to attain than a single-attribute concept and is a classic marker of higher classification ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The scored membership requires the conjunction of two attributes (the overlap), and distractors each satisfy only one attribute, so single-feature matching does not score.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.why: Conjunctive (two-dimension) categories are learned more slowly and reliably separate stronger classifiers than single-dimension categories.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty escalates from one shared attribute to a two-attribute conjunction with confusable single-attribute distractors, targeting the conjunctive-reasoning tail.
learning_science.source: Shepard, Hovland & Jenkins (1961), Psychological Monographs 75(13)

learning_science.why: Belonging can rest on relational or conjunctive properties, not just a single surface feature.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Higher bands use a spatial-relation conjunction (inside A and inside B) so membership is relational, not a single surface match.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

tail_precision_rationale: Because the keyed answer requires BOTH attributes, M-ERRTYPE reads which single attribute a wrong tap matched (a left-only or right-only near-miss), so a one-attribute match on a two-attribute item is a graded near-miss that places the child just below the conjunctive-classification cut. M-RULEID records whether one or both attributes were satisfied by the chosen figure, turning the item into a relational-complexity reading. M-RTFIRST indexes the rule-induction time before acting, and M-CONF on a subset removes lucky guesses via confidence-accuracy calibration.
age_rationale: A two-attribute conjunction requires holding two rules and testing candidates against both, which is unreliable in K-1; single-belonger K-1 classification is served by FLU-CLUB-01 and FLU-FAMILYSORT-01. 2-3 uses a near-single-attribute overlap with an obvious shared feature; 4-5 requires a genuine two-attribute conjunction; 6-8 uses confusable single-attribute distractors and a spatial-relation conjunction (matching the 6-8 GF-036 both-attribute item). Snap-to-overlap tapping keeps motor demands low from grade 2.

adaptive.content_range: obvious single-attribute overlap (grades 2-3) up to a two-attribute or spatial-relation conjunction with single-attribute distractors (6-8)
difficulty_levers: single attribute vs conjunction of two vs spatial-relation conjunction
distractor overlap: how many satisfy exactly one ring
adaptive.notes: Ring features and members are procedurally sampled with a uniqueness audit so exactly one candidate satisfies both rings; the overlap key gives automatic near-miss (single-attribute) coding and unlimited clones.

engagement_hook: Finding the one figure that fits into two clubs at once - dropping it into the glowing overlap where the rings cross is a satisfying both-at-once payoff.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that exactly one candidate satisfies both rings (no candidate defensibly fits via a third feature) so conjunctive scoring and near-miss coding are valid; pair color with shape/pattern for color-vision differences; keep ring features culturally common; large snap-to-overlap targets remove motor load; keep the confidence tap optional and non-punitive; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Buddy Pairs
topics_techniques_covered: figure_analogy: A is to B as C is to ? using concrete pictures or simple shapes; infer the A-to-B relation and pick C's matching partner (NNAT-style pre-reader on-ramp)
figure_analogy: simple A:B::C:? with one clear familiar change (e.g. big to small, one to two, solid to outline)
figure_analogy: two figures related by a rule, then a third with options; pick the figure completing the analogy (ICAR figural-analogies format)
figure_analogy: A:B::C:? with two shapes changing by one combined rule (size and shade) for older bands
one_liner: Two things are buddies because one changes into the other; the child taps the partner that pairs with a new thing the same way.
interaction: The top shows a buddy pair A and B joined by a link. Below sits C with an empty partner frame and three large candidate cards. The child taps the candidate that is C's buddy the same way B is A's buddy; it hops into the partner frame (tap another to swap) and the pair links up, then taps the big GO. Single tap, no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand traces the link between A and B (showing they belong together), slides down to C, and taps the matching partner so the two snap together with a spark. One unscored warm-up (big star links to small star, so big heart links to small heart) runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Analogical reasoning maps the relation, not the surface, from one pair to another.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each option set includes a surface-copy foil (C unchanged) and a wrong-relation foil so only relational partners score.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.principle: Relational shift is knowledge-driven, not stage-bound
learning_science.why: Young children reason analogically when the relation is familiar, so a concrete-relation on-ramp is appropriate at K-1 where arbitrary abstract transforms are not.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses highly familiar perceptual relations (big/small, one/two, solid/outline) with concrete pictures; abstract multi-transform pairs are reserved for older bands.
learning_science.source: Goswami & Brown (1990), Cognition 35(1); Gentner & Rattermann (1991)

learning_science.why: Beginning concrete then fading to abstract supports transfer of the analogy schema.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Pictures at K-1 fade to abstract shapes with size/count/shade transforms by grades 4-8.
learning_science.source: Fyfe, McNeil, Son & Goldstone (2014), Educational Psychology Review 26(1)

tail_precision_rationale: The keyed distractor set - a surface-copy foil (C unchanged), a wrong-relation foil, and on older bands an over-applied foil - lets M-ERRTYPE reveal exactly where the mapping broke, grading how far below the relational cut a child sits and separating a defensible near-miss from a random tap. M-RTFIRST captures the map-before-act latency typical of reflective solvers, and pairing it with M-RT credits reflection over impulsive first-glance matching. M-REV counts pre-commit swaps, distinguishing confident single-map solvers from guess-and-check at equal accuracy. Short cloneable pairs yield many stable samples without fatigue.
age_rationale: K-1 uses one familiar perceptual relation (big/small, one/two, solid/outline) shown between two concrete pictures, a condition under which young children reliably reason analogically (Goswami & Brown 1990); 2-3 uses one clear shape transform, 4-5 a single transform with confusable foils, 6-8 two combined transforms. Single large-tap options and no reading keep the youngest band accessible; the concrete-familiar-relation framing (versus the arbitrary abstract transforms of FLU-ANALOGY-01) is what admits K-1 here.

adaptive.content_range: one familiar concrete relation between pictures (K-1) up to two combined abstract transforms with relational distractors (6-8)
difficulty_levers: transform type: size, count, part/whole, fill/shade
adaptive.notes: Pairs generate from a relation grammar with relationally-keyed distractors; unlimited clones and clean difficulty control via relation familiarity and transform count.

engagement_hook: Buddies finding each other - the two cards snap together with a happy spark when the right partner is chosen, a matchmaking hook that makes the hidden relation feel worth finding.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Include a surface-copy foil so picture-matching does not score; ensure exactly one relational partner (audit for alternate valid relations); pair color with shape/pattern so color-vision differences do not mislead; keep K-1 pictures culturally common; large single-tap targets remove motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Copy Machine
topics_techniques_covered: figure_analogy: A is to B as C is to ? framed as a machine that turns an input into an output; infer the transformation from the shown A-to-B and predict the machine's output for C (NNAT transformation format)
figure_analogy: simple A:B::C:? with one clear change (e.g. big to small) - the machine applies one visible change
figure_analogy: A:B::C:? with two shapes changing by one combined rule (size and shade) - the machine applies two changes at once
figure_analogy: two figures related by a rule, then a third input with options; choose the output completing the analogy (ICAR figural analogies)
one_liner: A machine turns one shape into a changed shape; the child feeds in a new shape and taps which output the machine makes.
interaction: A friendly machine shows a sample run (A goes in, changed shape B comes out). Then C drops into the funnel, the machine whirs, and three candidate outputs line the chute; the child taps the one the machine produces (tap another to change), then taps GO. Single tap, no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand drops A into the funnel and the machine visibly transforms it into B at the chute (the rule is shown as an event, not explained), then drops C in and taps the matching output. One unscored warm-up (the machine shrinks a big circle to a small one, so it shrinks a big square to a small square) runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Casting A-to-B as an input-output process makes the relation an observable operation the child can run forward on C.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The rule is shown as a dynamic machine event and the child predicts the output, isolating relational inference from surface matching.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: The number of transformations that must be bound simultaneously governs analogy difficulty and separates ability at the tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Bands scale from one machine change (K-1/2-3) to two co-acting changes (6-8); output distractors are keyed to individual changes.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.why: Watching the machine transform once offloads the rule so the child can apply it independently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The demo shows the full A-to-B event; the warm-up fades to a self-run prediction.
learning_science.source: Sweller & Cooper (1985), Cognition and Instruction 2(1)

tail_precision_rationale: Outputs are keyed so each foil applies a wrong or partial transformation; on two-change items M-RULEID records how many transformations the chosen output correctly bound, cleanly separating one-rule from two-rule mappers at the same accuracy - a Halford-style relational-complexity signal that resists coaching. M-ERRTYPE labels the specific broken transform (no-change, partial, wrong-transform) as a graded near-miss versus a random pick, refining placement just below the analogy cut. M-RTFIRST indexes the infer-the-rule latency before predicting, and paired with M-RT credits reflective inference over impulsive guessing. Cloneable machine items give many stable samples.
age_rationale: K-1 uses one familiar visible change (shrink, add-one, recolor) demonstrated by the machine, which young children follow because the transformation is perceptual and shown rather than abstractly stated; 2-3 keeps one change with confusable outputs, 4-5 adds a subtler change, 6-8 applies two changes at once. Predicting a single output by one tap with big targets and no reading keeps K-1 accessible; the shown-transformation framing is what makes analogy tractable for the youngest band.

adaptive.content_range: one shown perceptual change on a concrete shape (K-1) up to two co-acting abstract transforms with per-rule keyed outputs (6-8)
difficulty_levers: transform type: size, count, fill/shade, recolor
output distractor keying: no-change, partial, wrong-transform
adaptive.notes: Machine transform and keyed outputs sample from a transform grammar; unlimited clones and precise difficulty via transform count and distractor keying.

engagement_hook: A whirring wonder-machine - feeding a shape in and predicting what pops out is playful cause-and-effect that makes the hidden rule tangible.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Show the transformation clearly enough that inference, not memory, is tested; include a no-change and a wrong-change foil so surface matching does not score; pair shade/color with shape; keep one visible change at K-1 so working memory does not confound; big single-tap outputs remove motor load; ghost-hand demo plus warm-up controls machine novelty.

name: Guest List
topics_techniques_covered: figure_classification: three figures share a hidden property; decide whether each new arrival also belongs (shares the property) and let it in
figure_classification: three pictures belong together (e.g. all things that fly); accept the arrivals that belong with them
figure_classification: figures share one generated attribute value (e.g. same number of sides); admit only those that fit, and require sharing BOTH attributes at harder bands
odd_one_out: several arrivals share the club's generated rule except one; keep the rule-breaker out (violation detection)
odd_one_out: four pictures where three share an obvious property and one does not; reject the one that does not belong
one_liner: A club's members all share a secret property; guests arrive one at a time and the child lets in the ones that fit and keeps out the one that does not.
interaction: A club frame shows three members that share a hidden property. Guests arrive one at a time at a gate with two big buttons - a green check (let IN) and a red X (keep OUT). The child taps IN if the guest shares the property or OUT if it breaks the rule; the guest joins the club or is bounced with an immediate settle or glow. After a fixed number of guests the child taps GO to finish. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand points to the three members (they go together), then a matching guest arrives and the ghost taps the green check (the guest joins, glow); a non-matching guest arrives and the ghost taps the red X (the guest bounces). One unscored warm-up (a club of round things - admit a circle, bounce a square) runs before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Deciding membership requires inducing the concept that unifies the members and testing each guest against it.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Members are positive exemplars only; the child induces the shared rule and applies an accept/reject decision to each guest.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.principle: Signal-detection separation of sensitivity from bias
learning_science.why: A yes/no stream lets hits and false alarms be separated so a cautious child and a yes-biased guesser are not scored alike.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Belongers (signal) and rule-breakers (noise) are interleaved so d-prime and false-alarm rate can be estimated per child.
learning_science.source: Green & Swets (1966), Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics

learning_science.why: Starting concrete then moving abstract supports transfer of the classification rule.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses familiar picture categories; older bands fade to abstract single- then dual-attribute rules.
learning_science.source: Fyfe, McNeil, Son & Goldstone (2014), Educational Psychology Review 26(1)

tail_precision_rationale: The interleaved belonger/rule-breaker stream yields M-DPRIME, separating genuine rule sensitivity from a yes/no response bias so near-cut children are placed on sensitivity, not guessing style. M-FALSEALARM isolates admitting a non-member (a commission error), distinguishing careful classifiers from permissive responders even at matched accuracy. M-ERRTYPE tags a wrong decision as a miss (bounced a member) or a false alarm (admitted a stranger), and which attribute a wrongly-admitted guest matched, so a one-attribute match on a two-attribute rule is a graded near-miss placing the child just below the conjunctive cut. Many quick accept/reject decisions give stable per-child estimates without fatigue.
age_rationale: K-1 uses a concrete single-attribute club (e.g. things that fly) with an obvious rule-breaker and big IN/OUT buttons; 2-3 moves to abstract single attributes, 4-5 and 6-8 require conjunctive (both-attribute) membership with confusable near-members. A binary accept/reject tap with no reading and immediate feedback keeps the youngest band supported.

adaptive.content_range: concrete single-attribute membership with an obvious violator (K-1) up to dual-attribute membership with confusable near-members and multiple violators (6-8)
difficulty_levers: single attribute to conjunction of two attributes
adaptive.notes: Club rule, belongers, and violators sample procedurally; the belonger-to-violator ratio tunes signal-detection difficulty; unlimited clones.

engagement_hook: Playing the bouncer - waving guests in or turning them away with a satisfying join-the-club glow or a bounce, a quick decisive rhythm kids enjoy.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Use positive exemplars that uniquely determine one rule (audit for alternate valid rules); pair color with shape/pattern so color-vision differences do not create false violators; keep K-1 categories culturally common; two large buttons remove motor load; balance IN and OUT trials so a fixed-answer strategy fails; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Mystery Gate
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: a hidden gate accepts only figures obeying a secret rule; the child DESIGNS their own test figures, feeds them in, and reads accept/reject feedback to induce the rule (active/selection concept learning rather than sorting a given queue)
visual_rule_discovery: two sets of figures - those the gate accepts vs rejects - implicitly define the criterial feature the child must isolate
inductive_reasoning: infer a general rule from self-generated positive and negative evidence, then apply it to classify new probe figures
figure_classification: after the rule is found, decide for each probe figure whether it belongs (obeys the rule) or not
one_liner: A magic gate opens only for figures that follow a secret rule; the child builds their own figures to test, watches which pass, then uses what they learned to judge new figures.
interaction: The child assembles a test figure from a small feature palette (tap to set shape, color, and count), then taps SEND to push it through the gate; the gate glows and opens (accept) or buzzes and bounces it back (reject), and the figure drops into an ACCEPTED or REJECTED tray. The child runs as many self-chosen tests as they like. When ready they tap I KNOW IT, and three probe figures appear one at a time; for each the child taps the OPEN gate (belongs) or the CLOSED gate (does not) to classify it. A hint lamp reveals one extra accepted example. Only the three final classifications are scored; the tests are the process record.
self_teach: The ghost-hand builds one figure on the palette (two taps), sends it, and the gate opens with a green glow and the figure lands in the ACCEPTED tray; it then builds a second figure that the gate buzzes and bounces into the REJECTED tray, making accept/reject obvious wordlessly. The warm-up uses a blatant one-color rule so the child feels the test-then-learn loop once before scoring.

learning_science.why: Letting the learner choose which cases to test is a distinct, more diagnostic paradigm than classifying a supplied sequence; selection strategies reveal how systematically a child isolates a variable.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child constructs and selects each test figure themselves rather than sorting a fixed queue, so the action log captures experimental strategy, not just classification accuracy.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.principle: Hypothesis space search / scientific discovery as dual search
learning_science.why: Rule discovery is a search over hypotheses guided by chosen experiments; efficient searchers run maximally informative tests.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty is set by how large the hypothesis space is (features that vary), and M-HYP scores whether the child's chosen tests are disambiguating (vary one feature) or redundant.
learning_science.source: Klahr & Dunbar (1988), Cognitive Science 12(1)

learning_science.why: Even young children can select evidence that reduces uncertainty; the quality of self-directed sampling is a strong reasoning signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The design rewards controlled, one-variable-at-a-time tests over confounded ones, surfacing the control-of-variables strategy without instruction.
learning_science.source: Schulz & Bonawitz (2007), Developmental Psychology 43(4)

tail_precision_rationale: Because the child designs their own experiments, M-HYP (informativeness of each self-chosen test) and M-EFF (tests used vs the minimum needed to disambiguate) isolate strategic inductive reasoners far more sharply than final accuracy: two children can both classify the probes correctly yet differ by running 3 controlled tests vs 12 confounded ones. M-PROG turns the test stream into an uncertainty-reduction curve (a dynamic-assessment learning-rate signal), M-PATH records the exact experiment sequence for evidence-model scoring, and hint-free discovery (M-HINT) is stronger evidence at the ceiling.
age_rationale: Designing and revising experiments demands generating hypotheses and holding a variable constant, which is unreliable in K-1 (served by the simpler FLU classification and series types). 2-3 uses a single obvious feature with immediate feedback; 4-5 uses a less salient single feature with more distractor dimensions; 6-8 uses conjunctive rules and can delay feedback until SEND batches. Tap-to-build with large targets keeps motor load low.

adaptive.content_range: single obvious-feature gate with a tiny feature palette (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive/relational hidden rules over many varying dimensions (6-8)
difficulty_levers: size of the hypothesis space (number of features that vary)
rule form: single feature to conjunction to relational
number of allowed tests before I KNOW IT
adaptive.notes: Rules and feature palettes are procedurally sampled; an automated uniqueness/identifiability check confirms the accept-set determines exactly one intended rule, so items clone at high throughput once audited.

engagement_hook: You are a scientist running experiments on a magic gate - every figure you invent is a little test, and the thrill of cracking the secret rule with a clever probe is intrinsically rewarding.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that the accept-set uniquely identifies the rule so M-HYP is meaningful; cap or de-emphasize test count so trial-and-error flooding is not rewarded (M-EFF penalizes it); pair color with shape/count so color-blind children are not disadvantaged; keep hints non-punitive but logged; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 to avoid a floor that would misread as low ability.

name: Odd Pair Out
topics_techniques_covered: figure_analogy: each pair shows A turning into B by a transformation; the child compares the transformation ACROSS pairs (a relation between relations) rather than completing one analogy
figure_analogy: A:B relations of one clear change (size, rotation, count, shade) and two-change combined rules for older bands
odd_one_out: among several same-rule pairs one pair follows a different transformation; select the pair that breaks the shared relation
visual_rule_discovery: infer the transformation each pair encodes and detect the one that is inconsistent with the majority
one_liner: Several before-and-after pairs all change in the same secret way except one; the child taps the pair whose change is different.
interaction: Four (K-8: up to five) pairs are shown, each a left figure with an arrow to its transformed right figure. Three or more pairs share one transformation (e.g., turn 90 degrees, or add a dot); exactly one pair uses a different transformation. The child taps the odd pair (the whole pair highlights) and confirms with a check; an optional confidence tap (sure / not sure) follows on a subset of items. Exactly one selection is scored per item.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sweeps left-to-right along each pair's arrow (tracing the change), pauses on the three matching pairs with a soft same-chime, then lands on the mismatching pair, which pulses and is tapped. The warm-up uses a vivid single change (all pairs get bigger except one that gets smaller) so the compare-the-change idea is obvious wordlessly.

learning_science.why: Judging whether two transformations are the same is second-order relational processing, a core driver of fluid-reasoning difficulty and of the gifted tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The task requires binding each pair's relation and then comparing relations, and difficulty scales with the number of dimensions the relation spans (Halford's relational complexity).
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6)

learning_science.why: Detecting the odd pair requires aligning relational structure, not surface features, which is the essence of analogical reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractor pairs share surface features but differ in relation, so surface matching fails and only structural alignment succeeds.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: The shared rule is never stated; the child must abstract it from multiple instances and use it as a comparison standard.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Three consistent pairs provide the inductive basis; the fourth tests whether the abstracted rule was correctly formed.
learning_science.source: Holyoak & Thagard (1995), Mental Leaps

tail_precision_rationale: M-RULEID captures how many relational dimensions the shared transformation spanned on correctly solved items (a same-turn rule vs a turn-and-shade rule), exposing the relational complexity a child can bind at once - a cleaner tail separator than a single difficulty index. M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a near-miss (child locked onto a surface feature and chose a plausible foil) from a random error, flagging latent ability just below threshold, and M-CONF adds metacognitive calibration to down-weight lucky guesses at the cut. M-RTFIRST indexes reflective encoding before the first tap.
age_rationale: Comparing a change across pairs requires abstracting a relation and holding it as a standard, which is fragile in K-1; the youngest band is covered by the direct analogy and odd-one-out FLU types. 2-3 uses one salient change with four pairs; 4-5 adds less salient single changes; 6-8 uses combined two-change relations and five pairs. Answering is a single large tap, so motor demand is minimal.

adaptive.content_range: one salient single-change relation among four pairs (grades 2-3) up to combined multi-dimension relations among five pairs (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number of relational dimensions in the shared rule
salience and type of the odd pair's deviation
surface similarity between odd and matching pairs (foil pull)
adaptive.notes: Pairs are generated from a transformation grammar; the odd pair is produced by swapping one transformation parameter, and a check confirms exactly one pair deviates, giving high-throughput cloning.

engagement_hook: A spot-the-impostor puzzle: three changes are secretly twins and one is a copycat that got it wrong - catching the fake change is a satisfying gotcha.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Guarantee exactly one pair deviates and that the deviation is relational (not a mere size/render artifact) so M-RULEID is valid; balance the odd pair's position to avoid position bias; pair color with shape so the shared rule never relies on color alone; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel compare-the-change format; keep confidence taps optional to avoid burden.

name: Clue Detective
topics_techniques_covered: nonverbal_deduction: clue cards each state a pictorial constraint (has a hole, not blue, three sides); the child eliminates every figure that violates each clue until one survivor remains

nonverbal_deduction: choose the figure where a spatial/attribute condition holds (a dot inside the circle but outside the square; the star above the box AND inside the ring) by accumulating constraints
nonverbal_deduction: deduce which figure is forced once all constraints are applied (constraint satisfaction by elimination rather than Latin-square uniqueness)
figure_classification: interpret each clue as a positive/negative property test applied to a lineup of candidates
one_liner: A lineup of figures hides one culprit; clue cards flip over one at a time and the child crosses out every figure a clue rules out until only the answer is left.
interaction: Six candidate figures sit in a lineup. Clue cards (wordless icons, e.g., a crossed-out blue swatch = not blue; a hole icon = must have a hole) reveal one at a time. After each clue the child taps the figures it eliminates (they dim and get an X); a mis-eliminated figure can be tapped again to restore it. When the child believes one figure survives all clues, they tap it in a final SELECT slot to answer. Eliminations are process-scored; the final pick is the keyed answer.
self_teach: The ghost-hand reveals the first clue card, then taps the two figures that clash with it - each dims with an X - and shakes its head at a figure that fits (leaving it lit). The warm-up runs a two-clue puzzle with obvious color/shape clues so the eliminate-the-violators loop is felt once before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Deductive constraint satisfaction / process of elimination
learning_science.why: Narrowing a candidate set by successively applying constraints is prototypical deductive reasoning distinct from inductive pattern completion.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each clue is a logical filter; the answer is the unique figure consistent with the conjunction of all clues, and the child must apply negation and conjunction correctly.
learning_science.source: Johnson-Laird (1983), Mental Models

learning_science.why: Efficient reasoners eliminate as soon as a clue falsifies a candidate rather than re-checking everything, showing model-based deduction.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The elimination log shows whether the child prunes decisively per clue (efficient) or thrashes, and M-EFF compares eliminations to the minimum forced by each clue.
learning_science.source: Markovits & Barrouillet (2002), Developmental Review 22(1)

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load managed by externalizing state
learning_science.why: Letting the child mark eliminations offloads working memory so the measured construct is deduction, not memory span.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Crossed-out figures stay visibly dimmed so the child reasons over the shrinking set without holding it in mind.
learning_science.source: Sweller (1988), Cognitive Science 12(2)

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY awards graded credit for the fraction of clues correctly applied even when the final pick is wrong, extracting tail information from one rich deduction puzzle (a single item behaves like several). M-EFF measures whether each elimination is exactly forced by the current clue (no over- or under-pruning), separating decisive deductive reasoners from guess-and-check, and M-PATH records the clue-by-clue elimination order for evidence-model scoring. M-ERRTYPE tags whether errors come from mishandling negation (not-blue) vs conjunction, and M-REV flags confident, targeted revisions vs thrashing.
age_rationale: Applying negation and conjunction across accumulating constraints is unreliable in K-1 (served by positive-match classification types). 2-3 uses two positive single-feature clues over four candidates; 4-5 introduces negation (not-blue) and three clues over six candidates; 6-8 uses conjunctive and relational spatial clues. Large tap targets and persistent dimming keep motor and memory load low.

adaptive.content_range: two positive single-feature clues over four candidates (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive and relational spatial clues over six-plus candidates (6-8)
difficulty_levers: clue polarity (positive vs negated) and logical form (single vs conjunctive)
relational/spatial clues (inside, above) vs simple attribute clues
how much each clue prunes (forcing more inference per step)
adaptive.notes: Candidate lineups and clue sets are generated so the conjunction yields exactly one survivor; an automated solver verifies uniqueness and minimum-elimination counts, enabling high-throughput cloning.

engagement_hook: A whodunit: each flipped clue card lets you rule out suspects, and the detective satisfaction of narrowing six figures down to the one culprit keeps kids leaning in.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Verify the clue conjunction yields a unique survivor and that clue icons are unambiguous (no reading) so the format is language-neutral; make elimination reversible so a mis-tap is not scored as reasoning error; pair color clues with shape/pattern clues; persistent dimming offloads memory so working memory is not confounded; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel elimination mechanic.

name: Ranking Ladder
topics_techniques_covered: nonverbal_deduction: integrate a chain of pairwise comparison clues (A beats B, B beats C) to deduce the single forced total order and read off the item forced into a queried rank
nonverbal_deduction: seat each figure in the one position consistent with all given relations, using transitivity to fix positions that no single clue states directly
one_liner: Clue cards each show one thing beating another; the child stacks all the clues together to work out the full winner-to-loser order and seats each character on the right rung.
interaction: A ladder (or podium) with empty rungs stands beside a row of characters and a small stack of clue cards. Each clue card wordlessly shows one character above/beating another (a see-saw tipping, a race arrow, or a taller-than bar). The child taps a card to spotlight the two characters it links, then taps a character and taps a rung to seat it (drag also works); the child may reseat freely until satisfied and taps DONE to commit. Harder items ask only for one queried rung ('who is on the gold rung?') by tapping a character. No numbers, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand flips two clue cards - one shows a bunny above a frog, the next a frog above a snail - then slides bunny, frog and snail onto the top, middle and bottom rungs in order and the ladder glows; the transitive chain is shown, not told, in under 10s. One unscored warm-up with three characters and two adjacent clues runs before scored items begin.

learning_science.why: The number of relations that must be integrated simultaneously predicts item difficulty and separates children by the relational load they can bind at once - a core fluid-reasoning limit.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items scale from 2 to 5 chained relations and each distractor rung is keyed so a near-miss violates exactly one relation, exposing how many relations the child integrated.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), 'Processing capacity defined by relational complexity', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6):803-831.

learning_science.why: Deducing an unstated ordering (A>C from A>B and B>C) indexes genuine relational reasoning rather than recall, and its development marks reasoning maturity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Queried ranks are chosen so the answer is fixed only by a non-adjacent, never-directly-stated pair, forcing transitive integration rather than clue lookup.
learning_science.source: Andrews & Halford (2002), 'A cognitive complexity metric applied to cognitive development', Cognitive Psychology 45(2):153-219.

learning_science.principle: Self-teaching via a wordless worked example
learning_science.why: A concrete animated ordering of the chain teaches the novel stacking mechanic without language.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand demo animates building one full order from two clues, plus one unscored warm-up, before scoring.
learning_science.source: Mayer (2005), The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-RULEID (the maximum number of chained relations the child correctly integrates) turns one ordering into a graded relational-complexity signal that a single right/wrong hides, placing children precisely by the relational load they can bind. M-HYP captures whether the child seats the fully-constrained (forced) characters first - an efficient deduction order - versus guessing then reshuffling, and M-ERRTYPE distinguishes an adjacent-swap near-miss (latent ability just below the cut) from a random order. M-RTFIRST marks the reflective planning pause of able integrators, while M-DIFFREACH escalates chain length to find the child's integration ceiling.
age_rationale: Transitive integration of multiple premises is fragile before roughly age 6-7, so K-1 is excluded (served by simpler classification and series types). 2-3 uses short 3-item chains with all-adjacent clues and a visible see-saw so partial ordering is perceptible; 4-5 adds a fourth item and one non-adjacent query; 6-8 uses 5-item chains, redundant or omitted clues, and two-attribute orders (order by height, break ties by width) that demand pure integration. Tap-to-seat with large snap targets keeps motor demand low.

adaptive.content_range: 3-item all-adjacent chains with a perceptible see-saw cue (2-3) up to 5-item chains with non-adjacent queries, redundant or slightly-underdetermined clues, and tie-break second attributes (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of items in the order (chain length)
number of relations that must be integrated
redundant vs minimal vs slightly-underdetermined clue sets
presence vs absence of a perceptual magnitude cue on each clue
adaptive.notes: Orders are generated as permutations; a clue subset is sampled and checked for a unique consistent ordering (or a named ambiguity); distractor rungs are derived by single-relation violations for M-ERRTYPE, and the solver computes the optimal seating order for M-HYP.

engagement_hook: Building a champions' podium from scattered match-up cards - each clue snaps two characters into their pecking order and the ladder lights up top-to-bottom when the whole ranking is right, a satisfying tournament-bracket payoff.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Keep clues wordless (see-saw/arrow icons) so it is not a reading test; make relations perceptual for young bands but remove the cue at the tail so success reflects integration not perception; large tap-snap rungs limit fine-motor load; ensure characters differ by shape not colour alone for colour-vision differences; the ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel stacking mechanic.
